justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon—one day, one week, and one month—are based on a combination of historical trends, prevailing conditions, and any known factors influencing the forecast variable. At each horizon, the central tendency of the forecast (i.e., the most likely outcome) remains consistent at 266.32 because the underlying data or conditions do not strongly suggest a directional shift. This assumes a roughly stable environment where past and current conditions hold. Over short periods, fluctuations are often modest, so the one-day and even one-week point estimates reflect an expectation of stability based on recent values.

The confidence interval widths expand as the time horizon increases, reflecting increasing uncertainty. For the one-day forecast, the narrow 90% confidence interval from 262.33 to 270.31 reflects only minor variations typical in short timeframes. Over a week, however, uncertainty grows because more variables, such as market volatility, external shocks, or random noise, can influence outcomes. The one-month interval is the widest (240.12 to 292.52) because uncertainty compounds over time. Longer horizons inherently involve greater risks, as less predictable or even rare events could have a more pronounced impact when given more time to play out.

Specific risks or events could push outcomes outside these intervals, though they are by definition unlikely within the 90% confidence bounds. Such risks might include major policy changes, unexpected geopolitical events, or significant shifts in market sentiment. These factors tend to be hard to predict but can have outsized effects, introducing tail risks that fall outside these ranges. Additionally, systemic shocks or events not incorporated into the forecasting model could lead to deviations. For example, if an unanticipated financial disruption or a natural disaster were to occur, it could materially distort outcomes far beyond what the current forecast captures.
